newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business May 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business May 20.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BROWN WARNS OF TOUGH BUDGET

Chancellor Brown says he is to have a tough tax-raising first Budget. He will tell the CBI about plans to improve the public finances and enlist business support in designing policies for the long-term health of the economy. Brown will also attempt to defuse the row over his proposed windfall tax on the utilities by presenting Labour as a pro-business party, keen to take advice from and harness the skills of entrepreneurs.
-- LOW-PAY CANDIDATE IN ONE MILLION STG A YEAR CLUB

Whitbread chief executive Peter Davis has been approached to head a government body that will advise on the level of the minimum wage. He also received more than one million stg last year. Jarvis surprised the City when he announced last December he is to retire as chief executive next month. He will receive a pension of 255,800 stg a year from the brewing, restaurants and pubs groups.
-- NORWICH HOLDERS SET FOR BIGGER WINDFALLS

Three million Norwich Union policyholders are to be sent offers to subscribe for extra shares. This could lift the value of the 300-share minimum allocation to with-profits policyholders by 160 stg due to rising financial sector share prices. 300,000 policyholders who are to receive 600 shares will gain twice as much. Norwich is to invite policyholders to subscribe for additional shares at a discount, unlike other mutual conversions distributing windfalls this year.
THE TIMES
-- BONUSES FAIL TO FEND OFF ATTACK ON BA STAFF
RELATIONS
British Airways have announced a pre-tax profit rise of 9.4 per cent to 640 million stg in the year to March 31. BA revealed a bonus package averaging 1,100 stg for its 58,000 employees.

Employees are to share a 94 million stg bonus, comprising 89 million stg in shared profits, plus 10 free BA shares each. This comes as members of the British Airways Stewards and Stewardesses Association protest over new terms and conditions, with a ballot result to be announced on June 27.
-- OFT INVESTIGATES DIXONS OVER "STRONG-ARM TACTICS"

Britain's largest electrical retailer, Dixons, could face a formal inquiry by the Office of Fair Trading over alleged "strong-arm tactics" to have rivals excluded from out-of-town shopping centres. The OFT accused it of using "unfair and anti- competitive" strategy to force developers of out-of-town centres to deny floor space to Dixons' competitors. Rivals claim that consumers are being forced to pay higher prices for electrical goods at shopping parks because of a lack of competition.
-- WATCHDOG CALLS TRUCE WITH SCOTTISH POWER

Professor Stephen Littlechild, the electricity regulator, has backed down from a dispute with Scottish Power that could have amounted to a 15 stg-a-year cut in household goods. Littlechild agreed to a six stg-a-year bill cut in order to end a legal battle between the two. The watchdog's office denied that this was a climbdown, saying he had ensured benefits for customers when the next stage of the dispute, a House of Lords challenge by the regulator, may have yielded nothing.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BROWN RECRUITS BARCLAYS CHIEF FOR WELFARE SHAKE-UP

Chief executive of Barclays Bank, Martin Taylor, has been appointed by Chancellor Brown to head a Whitehall task force charged with producing a blueprint for a modern welfare state. Taylor will devote two days a month to the welfare inquiry. Brown said that Taylor had the ability to find practical solutions that could make a long-term difference. Taylor is expected to produce a report in a year's time.
-- "NINE PENCE STG ON A PINT" WARNING

British pub company Greenalls warned that drinkers would have to foot the bill if the minimum wage was set at too high a level. Greenalls said that if the minimum wage was set at 4.10 stg an hour it would mean around nine pence stg on the price of a pint of beer. However, chief executive, Lord Daresbury, said he did not expect the Chancellor to set the wage at such a high level because of Brown's anti-inflationary credentials.
-- BOOTS' SHARES ROCKED BY FEAR OF FIVE BILLION STG US
LAWSUIT

Shares in Boots have fallen sharply after the news that it had been named, alongside BASF and Knoll, in an $8.5 billion lawsuit in the United States. Boots has said it was not a "proper defendant" and dismissed the idea of multi-billion dollar liabilities as "fanciful". BASF and Knoll called the claims unfounded and the size of the claim for damages as "grotesque". The lawsuit centres on allegations that the three groups suppressed a report on a drug that was no more effective than cheaper rivals.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- TAX REVENUE SURGE CHEERS CHANCELLOR

Figures have been released which show that the public finances were in surplus in the last month before the British general election. Buoyant tax revenues mean that the Treasury will be able to reduce its target for this year's public sector borrowing requirement in the Budget next month. Chancellor Gordon Brown, in a speech to the CBI, will promise to be tough on public spending and borrowing.
-- NATIONAL GRID FIGHTS OMBUDSMAN'S RULING

The High Court has heard that a ruling by the pensions ombudsman requiring National Grid to repay 46 million stg to its pension fund included an "astonishing proposition" which would prevent the company from ever reducing its contributions. QC for the Grid, Peter Crampin, said if the ruling were enforced it would mean the company would carry on accumulating huge surpluses in its fund without being able to adjust company contributions.
